justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift in what appears to be an asset or index currently trading near 1,075–1,080. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing level, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with little directional catalyst strong enough to move prices dramatically in either direction. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with a modest risk premium or recent short-term momentum. The one-month estimate continues that gentle upward slope, incorporating the idea that over longer horizons, assets with positive carry or growth expectations tend to drift upward, though the incremental gain I projected is deliberately conservative given the many things that can intervene.

The confidence interval widths widen at each horizon in a manner roughly consistent with the square root of time scaling for volatility. At one day, the interval is fairly tight because most of the relevant information is already priced in and the time window is short. By one week, there is meaningfully more room for macro data surprises, sentiment shifts, or liquidity events to move prices. By one month, the interval spans roughly 230 points, reflecting that a full calendar month can contain multiple central bank decisions, earnings cycles, geopolitical developments, or shifts in global risk appetite that compound uncertainty substantially.

Specific risks on the downside that could push outcomes below my stated intervals include a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — particularly around inflation, employment, or credit conditions — that triggers a repricing of risk. A liquidity event, such as a large institutional unwind or a flash crash, could also gap prices well outside the one-day range. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst like an unexpected policy easing announcement, a blowout earnings report, or a resolution of a geopolitical overhang could push prices above the upper bound.

At the one-month horizon specifically, I would note that tail risks are underrepresented even in a 90% interval. Black swan events — unexpected financial contagion, a sudden geopolitical escalation, or a policy error — are by definition difficult to price but could produce outcomes 15–20% outside my stated range. My intervals should be read as capturing the central distribution of plausible outcomes under roughly normal market conditions, not as hard bounds on what is possible.
